$comment: The demo topology: what `make demo` starts, in what order, and how it knows each one is up.
Order matters. The collector comes first because every role emits into it, and a role that
starts before it is listening loses whatever it emits in the meantime — there is no retry,
on purpose, because an event log that pushed back on the roles would be the coupling ADR
0003 forbids. The frontend comes last because it proxies to the collector and there is
nothing to look at until the roles are running.
The two agents come after the roles and before the frontend. Every role above them has either
answered its health check or been reported as a stub by then, so both run against a stack that
is up; what they produce is in the collector's history before the frontend starts, which is
what the 512-entry ring and the SSE replay are for — a browser attaching afterwards still sees
the whole transaction.
Two processes, and one would have done: cmd/agent takes -buy and -watch together and sequences
them, Human Present first. What decides it is what happens when the first one fails. A failed
purchase returns from that binary's run(), so a single process would exit before the watch had
authorised anything — a regression in the flow that already works would take the flow this
milestone is about off the screen with it, and the demonstration would show neither. Split,
each one fails on its own, and the Human Present path still fails on every `make demo`, in
front of whoever was about to take a screenshot, rather than only in CI.
agent-buy is started first so that the log holds one complete Human Present transaction before
the watch has anything to show. That is a preference and not a precondition: the runner gives a
process with no health check two seconds to fall over and then moves on, which in practice is
longer than a purchase against a stack that is already up, but is not a guarantee. An overlap
would be readable anyway — the two transactions carry different correlation IDs.
Each is named for the flag it runs, so an entry here and the binary it starts are one word
apart.
agent-watch states -poll where the merchant above it states -step and -step-max, because
those numbers only mean anything together. The watch triggers on the merchant's step
changing, so a poll longer than a step would step over the $210 the verifier is meant to
refuse and go straight from $240 to $189 — beat 5 of the built scenario, the one where a
verifier says no, would simply not happen. Issue #158 made -step and -step-max a range rather
than a fixed duration: each price now holds a random width drawn once from [-step, -step-max]
instead of the same thirty seconds every time — see merchant.NewJitteredSchedule — so what
-poll has to stay under is not the pair's average but its floor, -step itself, the shortest a
price can ever hold. One second against a three-to-six-second range is at least three polls a
step even in the worst case, and the whole watched-refused-bought flow now completes in
roughly twelve seconds — two transitions at up to six seconds each — rather than the two and a
half minutes two fixed thirty-second steps used to take. Shortening -step here still has to
bring -poll down with it, on the same terms as before: -poll must stay comfortably below
-step, which a reader can only notice if every number in the pair is in this file.
The four identifiers the agent can also be given are not restated, for the opposite reason.
They have to agree with cmd/merchant, cmd/credprovider and cmd/mpp, none of which is given one
here either — so both sides are the flag's default today, and a value written here could only
ever drift from the binary it names.
The merchant's `-catalogue` is not restated either, and on that same rule rather than by
oversight. It defaults to `../deploy/catalogue.json`, which resolves from the `backend` working
directory below, so a value here would say what the binary already says. What makes `-step`,
`-step-max` and `-poll` the exception is that they only mean anything together: the group has
to be read as one, which a reader can only do if every number in it is in this file. A path has
no partner.
agent-watch alone gets `-addr`, which is what turns the agent into a server: it serves the
console API of #137, so a browser can start a watch and poll where each mandate in it stands.
The flag defaults to empty meaning do not serve, so agent-buy above is byte-identical to what it
was — a Human Present purchase approved at the moment of purchase has no standing authorisation
for a console to track, and that process has no business listening. The watch this entry starts
runs inside the console rather than beside it, so the terminal and the browser are looking at
one run; frontend/vite.config.ts proxies /watches here, which is why the port is stated in both
files and has to move in both.
The merchant runs with `-demo-controls`, so `POST /demo/advance` moves its clock on by
exactly `-step` — the floor of the range, not a random draw of its own; see
merchant.DemoOptions.StepMax. It moves everything that merchant was built to read: the
prices, offer expiry, mandate expiry, challenge freshness, and the window its idempotency
store forgets records after. That is deliberate — the control says time passed rather than
that the price changed — and it is a property of how merchant.NewDemoService wires the
process, not of the endpoint. Off by default everywhere else: an endpoint that moves a
verifier's clock belongs in a demonstration and nowhere near anything real.
Nothing in `make demo` presses this control automatically — the automated flow lets the wall
clock carry the schedule at its own -step/-step-max cadence, which is what makes the twelve
second target true without anybody clicking anything. The control is for a presenter skipping
ahead by hand, and skipping ahead under a jittered schedule is imprecise in one specific way:
since a step's own random width can land anywhere up to `-step-max`, one press of exactly
`-step` is not guaranteed to cross it, and an occasional second press may be needed. That is
accepted rather than solved — solving it would mean the control asking the schedule for its
own next boundary instead of moving by a fixed duration, which is a bigger change than a
presenter's convenience needs.
It needs an `Idempotency-Key`, like every unsafe method here, and a repeat under the same key
replays the first answer instead of advancing again — which is what makes a double-clicked
button harmless and what makes two steps need two keys.
`implemented: false` marks a binary that is still a stub. The runner starts it anyway and
expects it to exit — which is how a stale flag becomes visible rather than silently wrong.
Flip it in the pull request that implements the role.

processes.name: collector
processes.summary: gathers protocol events and streams them to the frontend over SSE
processes.note: Demo infrastructure. Not an AP2 role and not a TAP identity party — see ADR 0003.

processes.name: surface
processes.summary: Trusted Surface — shows the interpretation and takes the user's signature

processes.name: merchant
processes.summary: Merchant — prices the route and verifies the Checkout Mandate
processes.note: Advance the schedule instead of waiting it out — a fresh key per step, since a repeat replays: curl -X POST -H 'Idempotency-Key: step-1' http://localhost:8081/demo/advance

processes.name: credprovider
processes.summary: Credential Provider — issues a payment credential scoped to one checkout

processes.name: mpp
processes.summary: Merchant Payment Processor — verifies the Payment Mandate

processes.name: registry
processes.summary: local agent registry — resolves an agent's key reference

processes.name: proxy
processes.summary: verifying proxy at the merchant edge — checks RFC 9421 signatures

processes.name: agent-buy
processes.summary: Shopping Agent — runs one Human Present purchase, then waits

processes.name: agent-watch
processes.summary: Shopping Agent — authorises once, then watches the price and buys on its own
processes.note: Human Not Present, beats 4 to 6: $240.00 watched, $210.00 refused with a signed receipt, $189.00 bought. Advance the merchant to see it sooner. It also serves the console API: GET http://127.0.0.1:8086/watches lists every watch, and a new one is curl -X POST -H 'Idempotency-Key: one-click' -d '{"prompt":"buy a flight to Palma when it drops below $200, this summer"}' http://127.0.0.1:8086/watches. GET http://127.0.0.1:8086/watches/{id}/attempts/1/presented is the four chains that attempt presented, each beside the verifier it was addressed to — it is what #21's Mandate Inspector reads, and the chains are deliberately not on the polled view

processes.name: frontend
processes.summary: three lanes, the Mandate Inspector and the Trusted Surface consent screen
